idiom_name: templated component with RenderFragment<TValue> template parameters
implementation_notes: Blazor ships the pattern as a first-class parameter type: a templated component declares one or more [Parameter] properties of type RenderFragment or RenderFragment<TValue> - a delegate that takes the state and returns a segment of UI - and invokes them in its own rendering logic (ItemTemplate(item) inside a foreach), which the documentation presents as the way to build higher-level, more reusable components. The classic structure is therefore replaced by the framework's delegate-typed template parameters; hand-write it only outside Blazor, where a Func<T, RenderFragment> parameter or an interface with a Render method is the manual equivalent. In WPF the same decision is expressed declaratively through DataTemplate resources instead of a function parameter.
pitfalls: A RenderFragment<TValue> parameter is null until supplied; invoking it without a guard or a default throws at render time, so optional templates need explicit handling.
The template delegate captures its enclosing component's render context; calling it from a different render tree (a dialog, another root) breaks cascading values and event handling.
Templates force the generic type parameter to be declared (@typeparam) and inferred at the call site; a missing or mismatched TItem produces unhelpful compile errors.

variants.name: WPF declarative data template (ItemTemplate/ContentTemplate)
variants.idiom_name: DataTemplate assigned to ItemTemplate or ContentTemplate, applied by DataType or a selector
variants.implementation_notes: In WPF the caller decides the markup by assigning a DataTemplate: the rendering function becomes a declarative template resource, and the framework applies it to each item of an ItemsControl (ItemTemplate) or to a ContentControl's content (ContentTemplate). The documentation states that what you specify in the DataTemplate becomes the visual structure of your data object, and DataType/DataTemplateSelector let the template be chosen from the state itself. Prefer this when the markup already lives in XAML and tooling or theming matters more than a function-valued API; the Blazor-style delegate remains the better fit for code-defined rendering.
variants.code_sketch:
<ItemsControl ItemsSource="{Binding Tasks}">
  <ItemsControl.ItemTemplate>
    <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type local:Task}">
      <StackPanel>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding TaskName}" />
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Priority}" />
      </StackPanel>
    </DataTemplate>
  </ItemsControl.ItemTemplate>
</ItemsControl>
pitfalls: A DataTemplate is selected implicitly by DataType; assigning it an x:Key overrides the implicit key and stops the automatic application - a documented source of silently unstyled items.
Bindings inside a template resolve against the item, not the page, so reaching for page-level state requires RelativeSource or ElementName indirection.
